title: Patrick (c. 5th century)
hookLine: kidnapped from Britain as a boy, enslaved in Ireland, he returns freely to the people who held him

cards: March seventeenth: green everything, parades, a river dyed green in Chicago. The Saint Patrick on the greeting cards comes with snakes, a shamrock and an Irish accent. Here's the surprise: he wasn't Irish.
And nobody has to guess about him, because he left two short pieces of writing in his own words. The longer one he called his confession.
It opens with him calling himself a sinner, very unlearned, the least of all the faithful. Not a legend. A man.

teach.b: Patrick grew up in Roman Britain. His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest, and by his own account he didn't take any of it seriously.
Then, when he was about sixteen, raiders from Ireland attacked his family's estate and carried him off with thousands of others.
He was sold as a slave and spent six years herding animals on a cold hillside, and that's where his faith woke up.
He writes that he prayed a hundred times in a day, and almost as many at night, in snow and frost and rain.
One night he heard a voice in his sleep telling him a ship was ready. He walked, he says, about two hundred miles to the coast, talked his way onto a ship, and got home. Free.
Safe. Family. Then the part that's hard to believe.
He had a dream: a man came to him with letters, and he heard the voices of the Irish, calling him to come back and walk among them again. So he went back.

Not as a slave this time, but as a bishop, to the island where he'd been owned, to the people who had held him. He spent the rest of his life there, baptizing thousands, facing threats and even arrest.
There were no snakes in Ireland to drive out, and he never mentions any.
The shamrock explaining the Trinity is a lovely story, but it only shows up in writing many centuries later. The true story needs no help.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Patrick on 17 March, a holy day in Ireland, and many pray the prayer known as Saint Patrick's Breastplate, though it was probably written later.

games.q: you're Patrick. you've escaped slavery and made it home to your family. then you dream that the Irish are calling you back. what do you do?
o: go back to Ireland, freely, as a bishop.
send someone else in your place.
games.why: he went back to the island where he'd been enslaved, and spent the rest of his life among its people.

practice: Bring to mind one person who hurt you; you don't have to do anything as big as Patrick did, and you don't have to go back to anyone who isn't safe.
Notice what happens in your body, breathe, and if you can, wish them one good thing, or, if you pray, pray for them by name. If no good wish comes today, let that be all right, and try another day.

orig.note: Latin: Patrick's name as he wrote it, meaning of noble or patrician rank.
